topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Prolonged seizures and rescue medication
blurb: Manage a prolonged convulsive seizure safely: recognise status epilepticus at 5 minutes, follow the emergency plan, give buccal midazolam correctly and know when to call 999.
question: Ruby, 31, has a learning disability and epilepsy. At her day centre she has a tonic-clonic seizure that is still going at 5 minutes. Her individual emergency plan says buccal midazolam at 5 minutes. What should the nurse do, and what happens if the seizure continues?

teach.h: When a seizure becomes an emergency
teach.body: NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more: provide resuscitation and immediate emergency treatment. A prolonged convulsive seizure is one that continues more than 2 minutes longer than the person's usual seizure, and is also a medical emergency. Repeated or cluster seizures (typically 3 or more self-terminating seizures in 24 hours) are managed as an emergency too. In plain English: time every seizure from the start, and know the person's usual length.

markers.label: Dose 2 if still fitting 5-10 min after dose 1

teach.caption: Follow the individual plan if it sets different timings for that person.

steps.label: Keep safe, time it
steps.sub: Cushion head, nothing in the mouth

steps.label: 5 minutes
steps.sub: Give medicine as in the individual plan

teach.caption: In hospital: IV lorazepam if IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available; seek expert help if no response.

teach.body: If the person has an individualised emergency management plan that is immediately available, give medication as the plan says (NG217 7.1.2). Plans state the medicine, the dose, when to give it, who is trained to give it, whether a second dose is allowed and when to call an ambulance. Without a plan to hand, give a benzodiazepine immediately: buccal midazolam (first choice in the community) or rectal diazepam, or IV lorazepam in hospital (7.1.3).

items: Check it is the person's own prescribed midazolam and in date, and that the strength (mg/mL) and the dose in mg match the plan: buccal products come in more than one strength.
Note the time the seizure started and the time you give the dose.
Place the medicine into the buccal cavity: the space between the inside of the cheek and the teeth.
It does not need to be swallowed; given into the middle of the mouth it works less well.
Watch breathing and colour; if the person stops breathing or the lips turn blue, call an ambulance immediately.
Give a second dose only if the plan or a clinician says so.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruby at the day centre
teach.body: The nurse starts timing as Ruby falls, cushions her head and moves furniture. At 5 minutes she gives Ruby's own buccal midazolam into the cheek pocket, as her plan says, and records the time. At 8 minutes Ruby is still convulsing, so a colleague calls 999 because she has not responded to the first dose. Ruby's plan allows a second dose 10 minutes after the first if paramedics have not arrived. When the seizure stops, the nurse places her in the recovery position, monitors breathing and checks her blood glucose.

teach.text: Two confusions. First, NICE's 5 to 10 minutes is the wait after the FIRST dose before a second dose, not the time from seizure onset. Second, 'call 999 if the first dose does not work' does not mean wait until after a second dose: call when there is no response to the first.

teach.body: Recovery position, airway and breathing checks, and stay with the person: midazolam can make breathing shallow and cause sleepiness and confusion. Think about causes: NG217 lists hypoglycaemia, eclampsia and alcohol withdrawal, and non-adherence to anti-seizure medicine. Be aware that dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures can look similar. After status epilepticus, agree an emergency plan with the person if they do not already have one and recurrence is a concern.

head: Check
Why
teach.caption: Stay with the person until fully recovered; they may be sleepy and confused.

items: Convulsive status epilepticus: seizure lasting 5 minutes or more.
Prolonged seizure: more than 2 minutes longer than the person's usual seizure.
Follow the individual emergency plan; otherwise buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community.
No response to the first dose: call 999; second dose if not stopped 5-10 minutes after the first.
Afterwards: recovery position, breathing, glucose, causes, and an emergency plan if none.

summary: You can now recognise convulsive status epilepticus at 5 minutes, follow an individual emergency plan, give buccal midazolam into the buccal cavity and escalate correctly. You know when a second dose is due and what to check after the seizure stops.

A.q: A support worker asks how long a convulsive seizure must last before NICE NG217 defines it as convulsive status epilepticus. What is the correct answer?
options: 5 minutes or more
3 minutes or more
10 minutes or more
30 minutes or more
A.why: NG217 7.1.1: convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, needing immediate emergency treatment.

whyNot.1: Three minutes is shorter than the NICE threshold.
whyNot.2: Ten minutes is the outer limit for a second dose after the first, not the definition.
whyNot.3: Thirty minutes is an older definition; waiting that long delays treatment.

A.q: Owen, 29, is having a prolonged seizure. A trained support worker is about to give his buccal midazolam. Where should the medicine be placed?
options: Between the inside of the cheek and the teeth
Under the tongue so it can be absorbed quickly
Into the middle of the mouth to be swallowed
Onto the lower lip so it runs into the mouth
A.why: Buccal midazolam goes into the buccal cavity, the space between the inside of the cheek and the teeth, where it is absorbed into the blood quickly.

whyNot.1: Buccal midazolam is given into the cheek, not under the tongue.
whyNot.2: Given into the middle of the mouth it works less well; it does not need to be swallowed.
whyNot.3: Dripping it onto the lip risks losing the dose and aspiration.

A.q: Liam, 24, has a learning disability and epilepsy. He has had a convulsive seizure at home for 6 minutes. His carers cannot find his emergency plan. What does NICE NG217 recommend?
options: Wait until 10 minutes before giving medicine
Give a benzodiazepine such as buccal midazolam now
Give his usual anti-seizure tablets by mouth straight away
Call 111 for advice before giving any medicine
A.why: NG217 7.1.3: without an individualised plan immediately available, give a benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam) immediately in the community.

whyNot.0: He is already in status epilepticus; delay is harmful.
whyNot.2: Nothing is given by mouth to a convulsing person; it risks choking and does not act fast.
whyNot.3: Status epilepticus needs immediate treatment; seeking advice first delays it.

B.q: Ahmed, 36, lives in supported living. His carer gave buccal midazolam 3 minutes ago as his plan directs, and he is still convulsing. What should happen now?
options: Give a second dose of midazolam straight away
Call 999 for emergency help
Give rectal diazepam as well
Wait until 15 minutes before acting
B.why: NG217 7.1.7: if status epilepticus does not respond to the first dose of benzodiazepine, call emergency services in the community.

whyNot.0: A second dose is considered if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first, and only as the plan allows.
whyNot.2: Giving a second benzodiazepine immediately risks respiratory depression.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays help for a seizure that is not responding.

B.q: Fatima, 40, has a profound learning disability. She received buccal midazolam 8 minutes ago, an ambulance has been called, and she is still having a convulsive seizure. Her plan allows a second dose. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait for paramedics before giving anything else
Give her usual evening anti-seizure medicine early
Give IV lorazepam from the ward emergency box
Give the second dose of benzodiazepine as planned
B.why: NG217 7.1.8: follow the individual plan or give a second dose of benzodiazepine if the seizure does not stop within 5 to 10 minutes of the first dose.

whyNot.0: Waiting leaves the seizure untreated when the plan allows a second dose.
whyNot.1: Oral medicine cannot be given safely during a seizure and acts too slowly.
whyNot.2: IV lorazepam is a hospital option needing IV access and resuscitation facilities.

B.q: Lauren, 33, has a learning disability. Her usual seizures last about 1 minute. Today a convulsive seizure has lasted 4 minutes. How should staff regard this seizure?
options: As a normal seizure, since it is under 5 minutes
As status epilepticus needing IV medicines
As a prolonged seizure and a medical emergency
As a likely dissociative seizure to observe
B.why: NG217 7.3.1: a prolonged convulsive seizure is one lasting more than 2 minutes longer than the person's usual seizure, and is managed as a medical emergency.

whyNot.0: It is 3 minutes longer than her usual seizure, so it meets the prolonged definition.
whyNot.1: Status epilepticus is defined at 5 minutes; IV medicines are a hospital step.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests a dissociative seizure; assuming so delays treatment.

C.q: Ben, 45, has a learning disability and diabetes treated with insulin. He has a prolonged seizure that stops after buccal midazolam. He is now in the recovery position with a clear airway and is breathing. What should the nurse check next?
options: Capillary blood glucose
Serum sodium level
A 12-lead ECG trace
Peak expiratory flow rate
C.why: NG217 7.1.4: be aware of underlying causes of status epilepticus, including hypoglycaemia. In a person on insulin a bedside glucose check is quick and changes treatment.

whyNot.1: Sodium may be checked later in hospital but is not the immediate bedside priority.
whyNot.2: An ECG is not the first check after a seizure in a person on insulin.
whyNot.3: Peak flow has no role after a seizure.

C.q: Grace, 27, has a learning disability and epilepsy. She has just been treated in hospital for convulsive status epilepticus and has no emergency plan. What should happen before discharge?
options: Prescribe buccal midazolam without any written plan
Advise her carers to call 999 for any future seizure
Agree an individualised emergency management plan
Increase her anti-seizure medicine to the maximum dose
C.why: NG217 7.1.12: after convulsive status epilepticus, agree an emergency management plan if the person does not already have one and recurrence is a concern.

whyNot.0: Rescue medicine needs a plan stating when, how and by whom it is given.
whyNot.1: Calling 999 for every seizure is not individualised and may not be needed.
whyNot.3: Dose changes are individual decisions and do not replace an emergency plan.

C.q: Tom, 30, has a learning disability. After buccal midazolam his seizure stops. Ten minutes later he is very sleepy, his breathing is shallow and his lips are turning blue. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Let him sleep, as drowsiness is expected after midazolam
Give him a sweet drink to raise his alertness
Recheck his breathing again in half an hour
Call an ambulance and support his airway now
C.why: Sleepiness is expected after midazolam, but blue lips with shallow breathing suggest respiratory depression. Call an ambulance immediately and support his airway and breathing.

whyNot.0: Sleepiness is expected, but blue lips are a danger sign that needs action.
whyNot.1: Nothing is given by mouth to a drowsy person with poor breathing; it risks aspiration.
whyNot.2: Waiting half an hour with cyanosis risks respiratory arrest.

reteach.title: Two clocks, not one
reteach.question: In a seizure emergency there are two clocks running. What are they, and what happens at each mark?

blocks.body: Clock 1 starts when the seizure starts: at 5 minutes it is status epilepticus and rescue medicine is given (or earlier if the plan says so). Clock 2 starts when the first dose is given: no response means call 999 now, and if it is still going 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose, a second dose can be given as the plan allows.

blocks.text: Do not wait for the second dose before calling 999, and do not give the second dose straight after the first.

explain.body: Status epilepticus: 5 minutes or more. Prolonged seizure: more than 2 minutes longer than usual. Cluster: typically 3 or more seizures in 24 hours. All are emergencies.

test.q: A man has three short self-terminating seizures in one afternoon. How should NG217 classify this?
options: Repeated or cluster seizures, an emergency
Usual epilepsy, recorded for the next review
Status epilepticus needing IV lorazepam
Prolonged seizures needing a second dose
test.why: NG217 7.2.1: manage repeated or cluster seizures (typically 3 or more self-terminating seizures in 24 hours) as a medical emergency.

whyNot.1: Clusters are emergencies, not routine events.
whyNot.2: Each seizure stopped on its own; this is not status epilepticus.
whyNot.3: Each seizure was short, so they are not prolonged seizures.

explain.body: If an individual emergency management plan is immediately available, give medication as it says (NG217 7.1.2). It names the medicine, dose, timing, who can give it and when to call an ambulance.

test.q: A woman's emergency plan says give buccal midazolam at 3 minutes. Her seizure has reached 3 minutes. What should the trained carer do?
options: Wait until 5 minutes as NICE defines status
Call the GP surgery for advice on the dose
Give the midazolam now as her plan says
Give half the dose now and half at 5 minutes
test.why: NG217 7.1.2: if an individualised plan is available, administer medication as detailed in the plan.

whyNot.0: Her plan is individual and takes priority over the general threshold.
whyNot.1: Calling the GP delays treatment the plan already sets out.
whyNot.3: Splitting the dose is not in her plan.

explain.body: Give a benzodiazepine immediately: buccal midazolam (first choice) or rectal diazepam in the community; IV lorazepam in hospital with IV access and resuscitation facilities (NG217 7.1.3).

test.q: A man has convulsive status epilepticus on a ward. He has a cannula and resuscitation equipment is at hand. Which first-line medicine does NICE recommend?
options: IV levetiracetam
IV lorazepam
IV phenytoin
Oral clobazam
test.why: NG217 7.1.3: use IV lorazepam if IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available.

whyNot.0: Levetiracetam is second-line after two benzodiazepine doses.
whyNot.3: Nothing is given by mouth during a convulsive seizure.

explain.body: No response to the first dose: call emergency services (community) or seek expert help (hospital). Second dose if not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first. Second-line IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate.

test.q: When does NICE recommend a second dose of benzodiazepine in status epilepticus?
options: If the seizure has continued for 30 minutes from its onset
Straight after the first dose to be sure it works
As soon as the paramedics arrive at the scene
If still fitting 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose
test.why: NG217 7.1.8: give a second dose if the seizure does not stop within 5 to 10 minutes of the first dose, or follow the plan.

whyNot.0: Thirty minutes is far too long to wait.
whyNot.2: Timing is set by the first dose, not by arrival of paramedics.
